The Sandbox ​

The sandbox runs a custom agent's Claude session inside a locked-down, disposable Docker container instead of in the Saidi process. Its job is filesystem and credential containment: an agent's Bash, Read, Write and Edit calls should not be able to reach another tenant's data on disk, and should not see the host environment that holds the database URI and the master key.

It is off by default. With SAIDI_SANDBOX unset, agents execute in-host and the only thing standing between a model-written shell command and your disk is the tool gate described in Modes & Permissions.

Request path when SAIDI_SANDBOX=1 ​

What is sandboxed, and what is not ​

PathSandboxed?
Custom-agent Claude delegations (runCustomAgent)Yes, when SAIDI_SANDBOX=1
Project-agent repo work (ask / work on a registered repo)No — runs in-host on the repo checkout
PRIME's own turnsNo
Mechanical task checksNo — see Checks are not sandboxed

So the sandbox is a boundary around one class of worker, not around the whole orchestrator. Turning it on does not make every command in a run containerised.

Two container shapes ​

Per-run container (pooled). When the delegation carries a runId, the pool starts one detached container for the whole run (docker run -d … sleep infinity) and drives each delegation through docker exec -i. Agents are separated inside it by directory — each works from /workspace/<agent>. The container holds no durable state: every directory it can write is a host bind mount, so it can be force-removed and lazily recreated without losing work.

Ephemeral container. Without a runId (main chat), each call gets its own docker run --rm -i container that exits when the command does.

Mounts in the per-run container ​

Container pathHost sourceMode
/workspacethe run's work rootrw
/run/assetsthe run's assets dir (prior files, uploads)ro
/run/outputthe run's output dir (deliverables)rw
/run/sharedcross-agent handoff notesrw
/run/agent-configper-agent CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIRrw
/agentsthe org's agent homesro

The ephemeral container gets one mount only: the delegation's workDir at /workspace.

A sandboxed agent's system prompt is rewritten to describe these container paths instead of host paths, and it is told to save deliverables into /run/output, which the engine sweeps into the run's assets after the delegation returns.

Isolation the flags actually give you ​

Every Saidi container — pooled or ephemeral — is started with the same hardening argument set:

FlagValueEffect
--userSaidi's own uid:gid (falls back to 1000:1000)Non-root inside the container
--cap-dropALLNo Linux capabilities
--security-optno-new-privilegessetuid binaries cannot escalate
--read-only—Immutable root filesystem
--tmpfs/tmp:rw,noexec,nosuid,size=512mThe only writable path outside the mounts
-vthe mounts aboveThe only host paths visible
--memory / --memory-swap2g / sameNo swap beyond the memory cap
--cpus2CPU cap
--pids-limit512A fork bomb cannot exhaust host PIDs

Read this list literally. It is a hardened container, not a VM, and the honest caveats are:

  • The container runs as Saidi's own uid. That is deliberate — a mismatched uid cannot read the workspace Saidi created for it — but it means the strength of the boundary depends on Saidi itself not running as root.
  • The network is not none in practice. The primitive defaults to --network none, but the worker has to reach the LLM, so the run path always starts the container on bridge (or host, if SAIDI_SANDBOX_NETWORK=host). That is general egress. The supported way to narrow it today is to point the host at a filtering proxy: HTTPS_PROXY, HTTP_PROXY, NO_PROXY (and their lowercase forms) plus NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS are forwarded into the container so the worker's calls go through the same policy.
  • Nothing here isolates the code the agent is reading. The workspace is a real host directory, mounted read-write.

The container's environment ​

The container's environment is only what the host explicitly passes — no host env is inherited. The allow-list is:

ANTHROPIC_API_KEY   ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN   ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL   ANTHROPIC_MODEL
CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN
ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_OPUS_MODEL   ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_SONNET_MODEL
ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_HAIKU_MODEL  ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_FABLE_MODEL
ANTHROPIC_SMALL_FAST_MODEL
HTTPS_PROXY  HTTP_PROXY  NO_PROXY  https_proxy  http_proxy  no_proxy
NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS

Plus CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR, which the pool sets to /run/agent-config/<agent>. Absent variables are simply not set. The database URI, the master key, every SAIDI_* variable and any other tenant's secrets are not among them.

If the run resolved a custom provider profile, that profile's env is merged over the base set: a defined value overrides, an undefined value deletes the base key.

Building and launching the worker ​

The thing that runs inside the container is a single bundled file. Two steps:

bash
npm run build:sandbox-worker
docker build -f src/orchestrator/sandbox/Dockerfile -t saidi-sandbox:latest .

The first step is esbuild: src/orchestrator/sandbox/worker.ts is bundled to dist/sandbox-worker.js as minified ESM targeting Node 20. Saidi's own source is inlined; npm packages stay external on purpose, because the Agent SDK spawns a platform-specific CLI binary and bundling the host's macOS build would not run in a Linux container.

The image is node:22-slim plus git, ca-certificates, curl, ripgrep and tini (PID 1, so orphaned subprocesses get reaped). The Agent SDK is installed from npm inside the image — pinned in worker-deps.json, which must match the version in the root package.json — so the Linux build of the CLI is fetched. The bundle lands at /opt/saidi/worker.js, and the image's own user is 1000:1000. No CMD is set; the command (node /opt/saidi/worker.js) comes from the launcher.

Set the image tag per deployment with SAIDI_SANDBOX_IMAGE; see Configuration for the full env var list.

Boot preflight ​

At startup Saidi probes docker info and docker image inspect (4-second bound each) and prints one of three things: sandbox off, sandbox on and runnable, or sandbox enabled but broken. An enabled-but-unbuilt image fails loudly at boot rather than silently on every delegation. When the sandbox is on and healthy, boot also sweeps containers labelled saidi.sandbox=1 that a prior crash left behind, and starts the idle reaper.

The host↔worker protocol ​

Nothing but JSON crosses the boundary — the host cannot hand a JS closure (a tool gate, an in-process MCP server, a callback) to a container. The host writes one SandboxJob to stdin; the worker writes newline-delimited events to stdout. Any stdout line that is not a JSON object is treated as log noise, never as an event.

EventCarries
statusmsg + optional detail (the exact tool call, e.g. $ npm test)
deltaone streamed text fragment
texta completed text block
sessionthe SDK session id, for resume
usagetoken counts, costUsd, and every model the turn touched
resultthe final report text + isError
errora fatal message

The job carries the task text (with any memory block already injected), the system prompt, the permission policy, the model, the actor name, the cwd, and a session id to resume. The usage event is what lets a sandboxed call be debited like any other, exactly like an in-host call.

Permissions inside the container ​

The worker rebuilds the permission gate from the serialized policy, so the tiers behave the same as in-host:

permissionAllowed toolsDenial message
read-onlyRead, Grep, Globread-only agent: "<tool>" is not permitted.
customexactly the agent's tools list"<tool>" is not in this agent's permitted tools.
alleverything the runtime offers—

Two further constraints apply to every sandboxed worker regardless of tier: ScheduleWakeup is disallowed, and settingSources is empty — no filesystem settings from the host or the user's global Claude configuration are loaded.

What the sandboxed path does not get, which the in-host path does: MCP servers. The worker is deliberately dependency-light and starts the SDK with no MCP servers and no agent-local plugin directory, so Saidi's own remember tool is unavailable inside the container. Agent reference material is reached through the read-only /agents mount instead.

Timeouts, reaping, and failure ​

LimitValueWhere
Delegation wall clock30 minutes (default)force-kills the exec/run and cleans up
Idle container TTL15 minutes, swept every 60snever reaps a container with a delegation in flight
Docker availability probe4 secondsboot preflight
tmpfs /tmp512 MBcontainer

Because killing a docker exec client does not stop the process inside the container, timeout and abort run an explicit cleanup. In a shared per-run container that cleanup is conditional: the container is torn down only when the timing-out exec is the last one in flight. If sibling agents are still working, just this exec client is dropped — their scratch survives, and a later call lazily recreates the container from the host mounts if it did go away.

A run's container is disposed when the run reaches done, cancelled or error, and when the run is deleted. Every tracked container is removed on process shutdown.

When the container cannot run at all — daemon down, image missing, timeout, worker crash, or a worker that emitted no result — the delegation comes back with an explicit non-retryable message:

Environment error (sandbox): <reason>. The agent could not run to completion —
this is an infrastructure/environment problem it cannot fix by trying again.
Do NOT re-delegate this task; report the failure to the operator.

That wording exists so PRIME escalates instead of burning the task's attempt budget re-delegating into the same broken daemon. A timeout reports the reason as the agent timed out (30-minute cap).

Checks are not sandboxed ​

A task's mechanical checks and a sandboxed delegation are two different containment problems solved two different ways, and it is worth being exact about which is which.

Checks run on the host, via bash -c in the evidence working tree — not inside any container, even when the sandbox is on. They also never pass through canUseTool, so no worker permission gate applies to them. What contains them instead is a static allow-list applied before the command is ever run:

ConstraintRule
ProgramsAn allow-list of inspection tools (test, ls, cat, grep, rg, diff, jq, npm, node, git, …). Anything else is refused
InvocationNo program by path — /bin/sh is rejected on its basename
SubstitutionNo $(…), backticks or ${…}
WritesNo redirection at all, and no tee; no sed -i
InterpretersNo -e, -c, --eval, --command, --print on node/python/python3
GitRead-only subcommands only (status, log, show, diff, rev-parse, …)
SizeAt most 3 checks per task, 500 characters each
Timeout60 seconds per check, 4 MB of captured output
EnvironmentThe worker env minus every variable whose name matches KEY, TOKEN, SECRET, PASSWORD, CREDENTIAL, AUTH or SESSION — and bash -c, never -lc, so a login shell cannot re-export what was just stripped

Every segment of a pipeline is validated, not just the first. A check that violates any of these is dropped, not run — which fails open to the model verifier, so removing a check can never turn into an easier pass. Exit code decides the verdict; the output is captured for the report but never parsed.

The practical consequence: enabling the sandbox contains what an agent does. It does not change what a model-authored check can do to the host. Both surfaces need their own posture — see Approval & Spend Guardrails.

Operating notes ​

  • Turning the sandbox on changes what a delegation can see. A prompt that referred to host paths will not find them; sandboxed agents are told about /workspace, /run/assets, /run/output, /run/shared and /agents instead.
  • Give a thrash-prone fleet more headroom with SAIDI_SANDBOX_MEMORY and SAIDI_SANDBOX_CPUS; the pid limit is fixed at 512.
  • SAIDI_AGENTS_DIR overrides which directory is mounted read-only at /agents.
  • If delegations start failing immediately after enabling it, check the boot line first — a missing image and an unreachable daemon produce different warnings, and both name the rebuild command.
